title: Creoles of color of New Orleans and their pushing into the ghettos
summary: Starting the scrapbook tour, Guesnon explains the Creoles of color, their wealth and trades, and how pressure forced them into the same ghettos as Black New Orleanians; his family spanned both.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Now, this tape will consist of mostly conversation. George is just going to get his scrapbook. A book where he put all the photographs and written down things in, you know. And he's going to tell me about all of that. Oh!

You see, this is the small part of them that are left. Look at the various colors. See, she's white as your wife is. Sandy, yellow-hand, blue eyes. Yeah, yeah. That's right. Here's another one. You see, well, these are what you call the Creoles of color. Creoles of color. Of New Orleans. Now, listen to this well. You see, before the Civil War, some of the wealthiest citizens of New Orleans were the world-renowned Creoles of color. Of French and Spanish heritage, these great land owners and slaveholders, if they were still functioning as a group now as in the past, would be rated today as a millionaire. Among them were to be found the best carpenters, plasterers, bricklayers, cigar makers, and musicians, considered neither white nor Negro. This outstanding group, a race within a race, with a fierce pride of their heritage and birthright, produced some of the most stalwart, outstanding, and respected citizens of the day. Among them, the well-known and legendary Tomy LaFont. Tomy LaFont. That's right, a plantation owner who left more than a million dollars to charity when he died. You can bet that when the song, Way Down Yon in New Orleans was written, that the Creole babies with flashy knives mentioned in the song was aimed and directed solely at the Creoles of color. Because among them were to be found some of the most beautiful women in the world, and that ain't no lie. They were all colors. They were white and coral and brown. You never saw women so pretty in all your life. They all vanished. They all gone. Most of them is in California now. They see now. And the envy of both the whites and the blacks. And it was this envy on the part of the whites that brought about a systematic pressure that began to force this once proud group, little by little, into the same ghettos with the blacks. And today, all of their true identity has become lost. But all one has to do is pronounce the above names. And they can see that nothing here pertains to any Negro at all, so-and-so. Or take it as so-and-so. All you got now is a small group left, but the memory of a great group that I was proud to call my people, the Creoles of color. See, now look at these names here. Edna Bibolo Sorina Sinigal. Romaniya de Marsilier. See, Buenis over here. Vera Falgut. And I mean, all these were Spanish and French, you see, some of the most beautiful people. And among them the greatest cigar makers, Placid, Brickley.
They were the most intelligent people.

That's right, I mean, you see. But, and they, like I told you on the part, they kept pushing them, pushing them, with the Buddy Bolden gang from uptown, and all that into the same ghettos.
